title: Probability of a timely vocal response in mother-infant interaction and later psychiatric diagnosis: A case-control study
one_line: Using ALSPAC video recordings of 158 mother-infant dyads at 12 months, the authors measured the probability of vocal responses within data-derived time windows and tested whether these predicted psychiatric diagnosis at age seven.
key_claims: Survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier over a 0.5-10 second sliding window) identified 1 second as the optimal maternal response threshold and 8 seconds as the optimal infant threshold.
A 10% increase in the probability of a maternal vocal response within 1 second was associated with a 17% decrease in the odds of any psychiatric diagnosis at age seven.
The maternal association was concentrated in ADHD and disruptive behaviour disorders and survived adjustment for maternal age, birth weight, maternal depression and socioeconomic status.
The infant 8-second response probability was generally not predictive of later psychiatric diagnosis.
Of 158 children assessed by the DAWBA at ~7 years, 103 were controls and 55 were cases (33 disruptive behaviour disorder, 16 ADHD, 25 emotional disorder, 6 pervasive developmental disorder).
limitations: Degraded 1990s VHS audio prevented analysis of speech content, pitch contours or infant-directed speech, so each vocalisation was coded as a binary sound event regardless of emotional quality.
Only six children had a pervasive developmental disorder diagnosis, leaving the null autism result essentially uninterpretable for lack of power.
Neither timing metric predicted autism spectrum or emotional disorders, contradicting a wider literature on reduced vocal interaction in autistic toddlers.
Observation was a short book-sharing session in an artificial clinic room, not naturalistic home interaction.
Case-control design with covariate adjustment cannot establish that maternal response latency causes later diagnosis.
open_questions: Would continuous naturalistic home audio recording over weeks reproduce the 1-second maternal effect outside a clinic setting?
Does response latency retain predictive weight once pitch, motherese and linguistic content are measured and controlled?
Is the maternal timing effect causal, i.e. does intervening to speed caregiver responses reduce later ADHD/DBD incidence?
Would an adequately powered autism subgroup reveal a contingency signal that this cohort of six could not detect?
